# Filtrations, Right-Continuity, and Completeness

<p class="unit-lead">How can the information available to an observer be represented as time evolves, and what regularity conditions make that representation stable under the operations used in stochastic analysis?</p>

::: {.learning-objectives}

## Learning objectives

After reading this unit, the reader should be able to:

- define a filtration and a filtered probability space
- interpret $\mathcal F_t$ as the information available at time $t$
- construct the canonical filtration of a stochastic process
- explain right-continuity and completeness of a filtration and
- describe why completion does not alter probability identities such as independence.

:::

## Filtrations as evolving information

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space. The $\sigma$-field $\mathcal F$ represents all events to which probabilities are assigned. In a time-dependent model, however, an observer generally does not know all of this information at once. The information available should increase as time passes.

::: {.definition}
### Definition: Filtration

A **filtration** on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a family

$$
(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le \infty}
$$

of sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\mathcal F$ such that

$$
\mathcal F_s\subseteq \mathcal F_t
\qquad\text{whenever }s\le t.
$$

The tuple

$$
\bigl(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\infty},P\bigr)
$$

is called a **filtered probability space**.
:::

Thus, for $0\le s\le t$,

$$
\mathcal F_0\subseteq \mathcal F_s\subseteq \mathcal F_t
\subseteq \mathcal F_\infty\subseteq \mathcal F.
$$

For an event $A$, the statement $A\in\mathcal F_t$ means that the information available by time $t$ is sufficient to decide whether the realized outcome $\omega$ belongs to $A$. The inclusion $\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ says that information, once observed, remains available later.

::: {.remark}
### Events versus random variables

The object $\mathcal F_t$ is a collection of **events**, not a collection of random variables. A random variable is observable at time $t$ precisely when it is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable.
:::

::: {.example}
### Example: Two coin tosses

Suppose two coin tosses are performed at times $1$ and $2$, with

$$
\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}.
$$

Before observing either toss,

$$
\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}.
$$

After the first toss, the observer knows whether the first coordinate is $H$ or $T$, so

$$
\mathcal F_1
=
\{\varnothing,\Omega,\{HH,HT\},\{TH,TT\}\}.
$$

After the second toss, the complete outcome is known, and therefore

$$
\mathcal F_2=2^\Omega.
$$

The sample space remains the space of complete two-toss outcomes. What changes with time is not $\Omega$, but which subsets of $\Omega$ can be distinguished.
:::

## The canonical filtration of a process

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a stochastic process. Observing the process up to time $t$ generates the $\sigma$-field

$$
\mathcal F_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:0\le s\le t).
$$

Together with

$$
\mathcal F_\infty^X
=
\sigma(X_s:s\ge0),
$$

this is called the **canonical filtration** or **natural filtration** of $X$.

The canonical filtration contains exactly the information generated by the process itself up to each time. In particular,

$$
\sigma(X_t)
\subseteq
\sigma(X_s:0\le s\le t)
=
\mathcal F_t^X,
$$

so $X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t^X$-measurable.

::: {.proposition}
### Proposition: Minimality of the canonical filtration

The canonical filtration is the smallest filtration to which $X$ is adapted.
:::

::: {.proof-box}
### Proof

Suppose $(\mathcal G_t)_{t\ge0}$ is another filtration such that $X_s$ is $\mathcal G_s$-measurable for every $s\ge0$. If $s\le t$, then

$$
\sigma(X_s)\subseteq\mathcal G_s\subseteq\mathcal G_t.
$$

Consequently, $\mathcal G_t$ contains every $\sigma(X_s)$ for $0\le s\le t$, and hence

$$
\mathcal F_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:0\le s\le t)
\subseteq
\mathcal G_t.
$$

Therefore every filtration making $X$ adapted must contain the canonical filtration. $\square$
:::

A filtration represents the information available to a chosen observer. It may therefore contain more information than is generated by one particular process.

## Right-continuous filtrations

For a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)$, define

$$
\mathcal F_{t+}
=
\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s.
$$

Since $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F_s$ for every $s>t$, we always have

$$
\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F_{t+}.
$$

::: {.definition}
### Definition: Right-continuity

A filtration is **right-continuous** if

$$
\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t+}
\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.
$$
:::

The interpretation is that an event which is observable at every time immediately after $t$ is already regarded as observable at time $t$.

The family $(\mathcal F_{t+})_{t\ge0}$ is right-continuous by construction. Indeed,

$$
(\mathcal F_{t+})_+
=
\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_{s+}
=
\bigcap_{s>t}\bigcap_{u>s}\mathcal F_u
=
\bigcap_{u>t}\mathcal F_u
=
\mathcal F_{t+}.
$$

::: {.example}
### Example: Information arriving immediately after time 1

Let $Z$ be a nonconstant random variable and define

$$
\mathcal F_t=
\begin{cases}
\{\varnothing,\Omega\}, & 0\le t\le1,\\
\sigma(Z), & t>1.
\end{cases}
$$

Then

$$
\mathcal F_1=\{\varnothing,\Omega\},
$$

whereas

$$
\mathcal F_{1+}
=
\bigcap_{s>1}\mathcal F_s
=
\sigma(Z).
$$

Thus $\mathcal F_1\ne\mathcal F_{1+}$. The information carried by $Z$ is available at every time strictly after $1$, but not at time $1$ itself.
:::

## Complete filtrations

Let $\mathcal N$ denote the collection of all subsets of $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable null sets. Thus $A\in\mathcal N$ when there exists $A_0\in\mathcal F_\infty$ such that

$$
A\subseteq A_0,
\qquad
P(A_0)=0.
$$

The set $A$ itself need not belong to the original $\sigma$-field. This is why the definition is not simply written as $P(A)=0$: the expression $P(A)$ is not defined until $A$ is known to be measurable.

::: {.definition}
### Definition: Complete filtration

A filtration is **complete** if

$$
\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal F_0.
$$
:::

Since $\mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F_t$, completeness implies

$$
\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal F_t
\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.
$$

### Why completeness is needed

Suppose $X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and another random variable $Y_t$ satisfies

$$
P(X_t=Y_t)=1.
$$

Let

$$
N=\{X_t\ne Y_t\}.
$$

Although $N$ is negligible, a noncomplete filtration need not contain $N$ or all of its subsets. It is then possible for $X_t$ to be $\mathcal F_t$-measurable while $Y_t$ is not. Completeness prevents measurability from depending on the chosen representative of an almost-sure equivalence class.

This matters because stochastic processes are frequently modified on negligible sets in order to obtain continuous or right-continuous sample paths.

### Completing a filtration

If the original filtration is not complete, define

$$
\mathcal F_t'
=
\mathcal F_t\vee\sigma(\mathcal N)
=
\sigma(\mathcal F_t\cup\mathcal N).
$$

Then $(\mathcal F_t')$ is a complete filtration, and the filtration property is preserved because

$$
\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathcal F_s'\subseteq\mathcal F_t'.
$$

::: {.remark}
### Why completion preserves independence identities

Every event $A'\in\mathcal F_t'$ differs by a null set from some event $A\in\mathcal F_t$:

$$
P(A'\triangle A)=0.
$$

Therefore $P(A')=P(A)$, and intersections are also unchanged up to null sets. If original events $A$ and $B$ satisfy

$$
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B),
$$

and $A',B'$ are completed versions of them, then

$$
P(A'\cap B')
=
P(A\cap B)
=
P(A)P(B)
=
P(A')P(B').
$$

Thus adding negligible events changes which representatives are measurable, but not the probability identities that define independence.
:::

## Key takeaways

1. A filtration $(\mathcal F_t)$ records information accumulated over time.
2. The canonical filtration $(\mathcal F_t^X)$ is the smallest filtration generated by observing a process $X$.
3. Right-continuity includes information available at every time immediately after $t$.
4. Completeness includes all subsets of measurable null sets from the beginning.
5. Completion stabilizes almost-sure modifications without changing probability identities.
